post.content: Opening question for the thread: Is The HVN in Knightsbridge a spa, a medical clinic, a longevity clinic or an aesthetics clinic? Its own pages use different descriptions, including "London's leading Wellness & Longevity Clinic", "Expert Skin & Hair Clinic Support" and "Book Your Skin & Hair Treatment Appointment". Has anyone here been, and what would you need to see before booking? Please say clearly if you are only going on the website.

Published on the clinic's own site: the team includes a GP-trained Medical Director (MRCGP) described as a global award-winning laser specialist, a second aesthetic doctor who also covers menopause and women's health, and a senior TCM practitioner. The site shows a CQC Regulated badge on every page, but I could not see a rating in the material I checked. Prices are published for many services (for example muscle-relaxing injections from £260, a £175 aesthetic consultation, and the 8R programme from £3,000), but most programme prices are no longer listed. Does a regulated badge with no rating reassure you, or does it raise questions?

I have been reading about the clinic's IV and NAD+ menu and I am not sure what to make of it. The site lists 14 IV infusions at £275 to £425 and NAD+ tiers at £350, £500 and £800, and the benefit claims are stated on the page. I am sceptical of drip marketing in general, so I would want to know what the evidence is. Has anyone here had one, and does the clinic's medical team give a clear answer when you ask? I do not want to comment on outcomes I have not seen myself.

For comparison, I usually go to the Harrods clinic for aesthetics and find it easy to tell who my injector is. The HVN lists named specialists, but I could not tell from the site which practitioner would treat me for a skin appointment. I also dislike paying for consultations before I know whether I will book treatment. The HVN charges £175 for a 60-minute aesthetic consultation, so I would like to know whether that fee is credited if I go ahead. Is anyone here sure about that?

A short checklist I wish I had used before my first private consultation, drawn from the threads on the HVN and similar clinics this week.

1. CQC registration is not a quality rating. It means a service is registered and inspected. Look up the location on the CQC website and read the latest inspection report, not just the badge.
2. Ask for the GMC number of the doctor who will actually see you, and check it on the GMC register. A team page is not enough.
3. Ask who conducts the consultation and who would carry out any treatment.
4. Ask for the cancellation and refund terms in writing before you pay, including whether a consultation fee is credited if you go ahead.
5. For IV or NAD+ menus, ask which studies support each claimed benefit, what the known risks are, and what differs between price tiers.

I am not a doctor, and none of this replaces advice from your own clinician. Where I could not find good data, I have said so. What would you add to the list?

Question for members and former members who have compared a fixed annual membership with pay-as-you-go.

I have been tracking my own usage for some months. Over the last quarter my use of the club has fallen, while the annual fee has stayed the same. Before I decide anything, I want to set out the numbers properly:

1. What is the real annual cost of selective use? Has anyone worked it out as (fixed fee divided by visits actually used), compared with booking individual consultations and assessments as needed?
2. Did anyone who switched to pay-as-you-go keep the same clinicians, facilities and priority booking? Or did the benefits shrink?
3. For clinics that offer a consultation fee credited against treatment (The HVN's £350 Discovery Consultation with £100 redeemable is one example in my reading), does that credit make a material difference to the total cost, or is it mostly a marketing point?
4. Has anyone asked the club for its pay-as-you-go terms in writing, and did they answer clearly?

I am not looking to criticise the club. I simply want to see whether a fixed fee still makes sense for someone who now uses it selectively. Real figures from others would be very helpful.

Thank you in advance.

James

comment.content: To be clear, CQC registration confirms that a service is registered and inspected, but it is not a quality rating. Ratings are published separately on the CQC website, so the absence of one on the clinic's own pages is worth checking rather than assuming the worst. What matters here is whether the inspection report is available and whether the Medical Director's GMC registration can be verified. I would want to see those credentials first, and a clear statement of which clinician will actually see the patient at consultation.

Hello, and thank you for opening this thread so carefully. I have never been to the HVN and I have not booked anything. I am going only on the public website, so I can't speak to what the rooms or the staff are actually like. From what I have read, the wording does shift between wellness, medical and aesthetic, and that alone makes me want to slow down. Before I committed to anything, I would want to know who would actually be treating me, what their training is in that specific area, what the evidence is for what I'd be paying for, and what happens if I decide not to go ahead. I have also learned to ask for the full cost of a programme in writing, not just the first price. Curious to hear from anyone who has been. Breathe slowly, everyone.

I have not been. I am going on the clinic's website only, so please weigh what follows accordingly.

Before booking, I would want to see the following in writing:
1. Which services are regulated, and the legal entity that provides each one. A CQC badge alone tells me little. I would check the location's registration and latest inspection rating.
2. The name and GMC number of the doctor responsible for each treatment, not only a team page.
3. Confirmation of indemnity cover.
4. Cancellation and refund terms for the consultation, and whether the fee is credited if I go ahead.
5. A named coordinator rather than a generic inbox.

On the positioning question: the site mixes aesthetics, IV therapy, TCM and spa treatments. Each one needs its own regulatory footing. The paperwork should come before the promise.

Has anyone been given the written terms for a consultation? I would be glad to see them.

I cannot confirm this from personal experience, so I would not rely on my view alone. What matters here is that the terms are stated in writing before any payment. The questions I would put to the clinic are whether the £175 aesthetic consultation is credited against any treatment booked within a set period, who the treating practitioner would be, and whether that person is the one who conducts the consultation. A named clinician and a written refund policy would settle most of my concerns. Has anyone received the written terms?

On the public information available, I have not found published evidence supporting the specific benefit claims on the IV and NAD+ pages, so I can't assess them yet. For each infusion, it would be worth asking the clinic directly which studies support the claimed benefit, what the known risks are, who prescribes it, and how it is monitored. The evidence here is limited for many drip claims, and the page does not say much about that. I would also ask what actually differs between the NAD+ tiers in dose and inclusions, since the price gap is large. Would be interested to hear from anyone who has had a written answer on this.

I cannot confirm this from the materials I have checked, so I would not rely on it either way. Worth asking the clinic to put in writing whether the £175 aesthetic consultation fee is credited against any treatment you book, and which named practitioner would see you for the appointment. Based on what I have read, that is not clear on the site. Happy to hear from anyone who has had this confirmed directly.

Let us be precise about what would count as evidence here. For NAD+ or high-dose vitamin infusions, I would want to see the trial design, the population studied, the sample size, the comparator (placebo or usual care), and the length of follow-up. The outcome matters too. A patient-relevant outcome such as energy, function or quality of life is more useful than a blood level that the infusion itself has changed. If the clinic has published any of this, I would be glad to read it. If not, the £350 to £800 tiers need a clear written explanation of what actually differs between them in dose and inclusions. The evidence is thin, and I would rather say so plainly than guess.

Agreed on the distinction. The CQC badge tells us the service is registered, not how it rated. I have not yet checked the location's inspection report on the CQC website, so I am not drawing a conclusion from the missing rating. My next step is to look up the registered location and the report, and to check the Medical Director's GMC entry. I will update this post with what I find, including if the rating turns out to be straightforward. The page does not say which clinician would see a patient at consultation, so that is the question I would put to the clinic first.

Honestly, I can only speak from my own experience at a different clinic. I have been a regular client at the Harrods clinic for several years, and recently I was asked to pay for a consultation again before a follow-up with an injector I already book with. The fee was not credited against the treatment, and the reason was not explained clearly at the time. I have noted the dates, the amount and who handled the booking, and I am asking for the policy in writing before my next visit. A consultation fee can be fair if it covers the clinician's time, but it should be stated up front, along with whether it counts towards treatment. Has anyone at the HVN had a written answer on the crediting question?

Fair enough, this is a sensible list. I would add one thing: ask the clinic to confirm in writing who will carry out the treatment itself, not just who did the consultation. I have had a booking where the named injector changed without much notice, and I only found out on the day. Honestly, a clinic that can say that plainly is a clinic I trust more. Has anyone found a clinic that answers the 'who actually did it?' question without being asked twice?

A useful list. I would add two points.

6. Ask for a single named coordinator for the whole relationship, not a generic inbox. Get the name and direct contact in writing, and check how quickly they answer a simple factual question before you commit.

7. For any assessment that produces health data, ask what is measured, what the results can and cannot tell you, who holds the data, how long it is kept, and whether you can have a copy. Ask too what happens to the data if you stop using the service.

Paperwork before the promise.

Thank you for pulling this together, it's a really useful list. I would add one thing: ask for the full cost of any programme in writing before the first consultation, not only the price of the first appointment. Several of the threads this week suggest the total can be much higher than the opening figure. I would also ask whether anyone is pushing a decision on a timeline. If you are planning a wedding or going through fertility treatment, it is easy to feel rushed, and a good clinic should be happy for you to take a few days and come back with questions. Nobody should have to decide under pressure. Breathe slowly, and take your time with it.

Useful list. I would add one item: ask for the baseline test panel in writing, including the reference ranges the clinic uses and which lab runs the tests. For any programme, I want three answers in writing before I pay: what is tested at baseline, how progress is measured, and what happens if the numbers do not move. If a clinic cannot answer those, that tells you most of what you need to know. Show me the panel.

On your question: a regulated badge with no rating does not reassure me, but it does not alarm me either. Registration means the service is known to the regulator, and the rating is a separate, public record. I would check the location's latest CQC inspection report before drawing any conclusion. The point I would press is who the treating clinician is for each service. A Medical Director's GMC number should be verifiable on the register, and the patient should be told in writing who will see them. Missing published programme prices are a fair question to put to the clinic too.

A useful list. I would add one item that is easy to overlook:

6. Ask for the total cost of the whole pathway in writing, not only the first fee. That means the consultation, any diagnostics, the treatment itself, follow-up appointments, and what happens if the programme is paused or cancelled part way through. Compare that figure with the same tests and consultations booked individually elsewhere.

I keep a simple spreadsheet of what I actually pay and what each appointment delivers. Once the numbers are laid side by side, most of the questions in the thread answer themselves.

Thank you for setting this out so clearly.

James

I have not used a fixed-fee club, so I cannot offer real figures. Your method in point 1 is a sensible starting point, but it treats each visit as equal. It would be worth also recording which visits you would have paid for anyway and which you only booked because they were included. On point 3, I would check the exact wording of any consultation credit against the clinic's own published terms before relying on it. In my own notes I have the £350 Discovery Consultation at The HVN, but I have not verified a £100 redeemable credit, so I would not use that figure in the sums until it is confirmed in writing. Worth asking the club for the pay-as-you-go terms in writing first, then comparing the two totals side by side.

I would add one point to your list: the fee for the pay-as-you-go option, and whether it changes once you have used a set number of visits.

On the membership question, I would ask for three things in writing before comparing totals:
1. The full annual cost, including any joining or renewal charges.
2. The pay-as-you-go rate for each service you actually use, with the same clinician and facilities.
3. The cancellation and notice terms for leaving the membership, and whether any unused benefit is refunded.

A fixed fee can still make sense for someone who uses a service regularly. For someone who now uses it selectively, the paperwork should show the break-even point. I would not rely on the club's own summary of its value.

One thing to check alongside the inspection report: the CQC location page lists the regulated activities the location is registered for. That tells you whether services such as injectables, IV therapy or the TCM work are actually covered by the registration, which a badge on the homepage does not show. If a service is not on that list, the badge is not reassurance for that service. I have not checked this for the HVN myself, so I would not draw a conclusion yet. Has anyone looked at the location page?

Thank you, James, this is a clear way to set it out. I would add one thing from my own experience of client budgets: a fixed fee can quietly create pressure to keep using a service after it has stopped serving you. If the numbers show you are using it less, that is useful information rather than a failure. I would ask for the pay-as-you-go terms in writing, as you plan to, and then decide on the figures alone, without the sense that you have to get your money's worth. Breathe slowly, and be kind to yourself about the decision.

A practical way to test the fixed fee is to work out the break-even number of visits: the annual fee divided by the pay-as-you-go price for the same service, with the same clinician and facilities. If you use fewer visits than that figure, the fixed fee is costing you more than paying as you go. I would only count visits you would have paid for anyway. Visits that were free only because they were included should not count as savings.

I have not used a fixed-fee club, so I cannot offer real figures of my own. I would also ask for the pay-as-you-go rates and the cancellation terms in writing before deciding. Once both totals are on paper, the comparison is much easier to make calmly. Thank you for setting it out so clearly.

Good to see someone asking for the evidence before the drip. Most vitamin infusions mainly change circulating levels, and those changes are usually short-lived, so a higher blood level is not the same as a patient benefit. For each of the 14 infusions and the NAD+ tiers, I would want three things in writing: the outcome being claimed, how it is measured at baseline and at follow-up, and what the known risks are, including infection and fluid overload when administration is poor. What is the endpoint for the £800 tier, and what separates it from the £350 one?

Thank you for setting out your experience. It is the kind of first-hand account I find more useful than the website copy.

Two points, for clarity.

1. The £175 aesthetic consultation and the £350 Discovery Consultation (with £100 redeemable against functional medicine packages) appear to be different products. Before anyone relies on a credit figure, it would help to know which one each of us was quoted, and in writing.
2. On your question about crediting: I have not had a booking here, so I cannot confirm it. The clinic should be able to state the terms in a single document, covering whether the fee is credited, the time limit for redeeming it, and the refund position if you decide not to proceed.

I would ask for that document before paying, not after. Has anyone received it?

James

Agree with the point about CQC registration not being a rating. For me the more practical question is the one you raised in the post: which clinician would actually see me at consultation? A Medical Director's GMC number is useful, but I would want the name of the person who would do my consultation and the person who would carry out any treatment, confirmed in writing. Honestly, a clinic that cannot answer 'who actually did it?' plainly would make me walk away. Has anyone had that confirmed by the clinic directly?

A sensible list. I would add one point from the NHS side: before paying for any private assessment, check what your GP can offer free. In England, the NHS Health Check (for adults aged 40 to 74) covers blood pressure, cholesterol, kidney function and diabetes risk, which overlaps with much of what is sold as a longevity baseline. If a private panel is recommended, ask which result would change the clinic's management, and who will explain any abnormal result to you afterwards. Several patients I have seen were handed a printout with no one to interpret it. Let us be precise about what the test can and cannot tell you.

I have not had one, so I can't comment on how it feels. On the evidence, a practical starting point is to search PubMed and the Cochrane Library for the specific infusion or NAD+ and read what the trials measured, how many people took part, and whether there was a placebo group. Many of the claims on menus like this come from small studies or from blood levels rather than outcomes patients care about, such as energy or quality of life. I am not a medical professional, so this is only a way to check the claims, not advice. If the clinic can point to the studies behind each benefit claim, that would be a good sign. If it cannot, I would treat the claim as unproven.

I have not seen the terms either, so I would not rely on anecdote in either direction. I would ask the clinic for three things in writing before paying: whether the £175 aesthetic consultation is credited against any treatment booked within a set period, the name of the practitioner who will see you and the one who will carry out any treatment, and the cancellation terms. Paperwork before the promise.

To be clear, this is a sound list. I would add one point: ask for the consultation summary in writing, stating the findings, what the clinic recommends, and what it does not recommend. What matters here is that a clinic should be able to say what its assessment cannot tell you, and whether any recommendation is necessary at all. I would want to see the credentials of the physician before anything else.

I would not rely on either the website or anecdote here. The useful distinction is between the £175 aesthetic consultation and the £350 Discovery Consultation, which appear to be different products. Before paying, I would ask for a single written statement covering whether the fee is credited, the time limit for any credit, and the refund position if I decide not to proceed. Once that is in hand, I would compare it with the published terms. Has anyone actually received that document from the clinic?

I have not been, and I am going only on the public pages, so please weigh this accordingly. The TCM part of the offer is the one I would check most carefully. Before anyone books it, I would ask: what is the practitioner's recognised qualification, which professional body they are registered with, and whether they hold professional indemnity insurance. If any needles are used, I would ask whether they are single-use and sterile, how they are disposed of, and what the clinic does about infection control. I would also ask what the TCM treatment is for, what the evidence says about that specific use, and what a realistic expectation looks like. For what it is worth, I have found acupuncture easier to think about as a possible help for stress and comfort than as something that changes clinical outcomes. Has anyone asked these questions directly and got written answers?

I have not had an infusion and would not describe the menu as evidence. Before anyone pays, I would want the following in writing for the NAD+ tiers in particular:

1. The outcome claimed for each tier, and how it is measured at baseline and follow-up.
2. The studies behind that claim: population, sample size, comparator (placebo or usual care) and length of follow-up.
3. What actually differs between the £350, £500 and £800 tiers in dose, duration and inclusions.
4. The named clinician who prescribes and monitors the infusion.

If the clinic can produce those, the price gap can be judged on its merits. If not, I would treat the claims as unproven. Has anyone received a written answer of this kind?

James

Thank you, this is a really useful list. I would add one practical point: ask for the full timeline in writing, week by week. Which session falls in which week, when each step should finish, and what happens if you miss one. I am planning my wedding prep in five-week blocks, and a plan that cannot show its dates on paper is very hard to fit around work. Has anyone had a clinic put the whole schedule and total cost on one page?

Agree with the request for a written summary, but I'd put the endpoints before the dates and the price. Before committing to any programme I'd want three things in writing: what is measured at baseline, how progress is measured and against what threshold, and what happens if the numbers do not move. A one-page schedule with total cost is a fair ask, but it doesn't tell you whether the programme does anything. Show me the panel first.

Honestly, the break-even approach is the sensible way to test a fixed fee. I would only count the visits you would have paid for anyway, as you say. Has anyone had the pay-as-you-go rates and cancellation terms confirmed in writing before committing? That is the figure I would want to see first.

Agree that the break-even test is the right way to judge a fixed fee. Before running the sum, I'd want two things in writing: the per-visit pay-as-you-go rate, and whether both options include the same diagnostic panel. If the panel differs, the comparison isn't like for like. Cancellation terms too. Show me the panel.

Agree the break-even test is the right way to judge a fixed fee, but only if both options include the same diagnostic panel. If the panel differs, the comparison isn't like for like. Two questions before I run the numbers: what is the per-visit pay-as-you-go rate, in writing, and what are the cancellation terms? Also, what is the endpoint, and which markers would show whether anything moved? Show me the panel.

Fair enough on the break-even test, but I would want the per-visit rate in writing before running any sums. Does the fixed fee include the same diagnostic panel as the pay-as-you-go option? If it doesn't, the comparison isn't like for like. Are cancellation terms set out anywhere too? Clear prices, honest answers, that's all I want.

Agreed that break-even is the right test for a fixed fee, provided the comparison is like for like. Before I run the numbers, I would like clarity on the following:

1. What is the per-visit pay-as-you-go rate, in writing, and does it include the same diagnostic panel as the membership?
2. What are the cancellation terms for both options?
3. What is the intended endpoint of the programme, and which markers would show whether anything has actually moved?

If any members have switched to pay-as-you-go, I would be interested in their real annual totals for selective use. I will share the anonymised figures once I have them in my spreadsheet.

Regards,
James

{"content": "To be clear, CQC registration confirms that a service is registered and inspected, but it is not a quality rating. Ratings are published separately on the CQC website, so the absence of one on the clinic's own pages is worth checking rather than assuming the worst. What matters here is whether the inspection report is available and whether the Medical Director's GMC registration can be verified. I would want to see those credentials first, and a clear statement of which clinician will actually see the patient at consultation.", "comment_id": 1}

{"content": "Hello, and thank you for opening this thread so carefully. I have never been to the HVN and I have not booked anything. I am going only on the public website, so I can't speak to what the rooms or the staff are actually like. From what I have read, the wording does shift between wellness, medical and aesthetic, and that alone makes me want to slow down. Before I committed to anything, I would want to know who would actually be treating me, what their training is in that specific area, what the evidence is for what I'd be paying for, and what happens if I decide not to go ahead. I have also learned to ask for the full cost of a programme in writing, not just the first price. Curious to hear from anyone who has been. Breathe slowly, everyone.", "comment_id": 2}
{"post_id": 3, "like_id": 1}

{"content": "I have not been. I am going on the clinic's website only, so please weigh what follows accordingly.

Before booking, I would want to see the following in writing:
1. Which services are regulated, and the legal entity that provides each one. A CQC badge alone tells me little. I would check the location's registration and latest inspection rating.
2. The name and GMC number of the doctor responsible for each treatment, not only a team page.
3. Confirmation of indemnity cover.
4. Cancellation and refund terms for the consultation, and whether the fee is credited if I go ahead.
5. A named coordinator rather than a generic inbox.

On the positioning question: the site mixes aesthetics, IV therapy, TCM and spa treatments. Each one needs its own regulatory footing. The paperwork should come before the promise.

Has anyone been given the written terms for a consultation? I would be glad to see them.", "comment_id": 3}

{"content": "Let us be precise about what would count as evidence here. For NAD+ or high-dose vitamin infusions, I would want to see the trial design, the population studied, the sample size, the comparator (placebo or usual care), and the length of follow-up. The outcome matters too. A patient-relevant outcome such as energy, function or quality of life is more useful than a blood level that the infusion itself has changed. If the clinic has published any of this, I would be glad to read it. If not, the \u00a3350 to \u00a3800 tiers need a clear written explanation of what actually differs between them in dose and inclusions. The evidence is thin, and I would rather say so plainly than guess.", "comment_id": 7}

{"content": "A short checklist I wish I had used before my first private consultation, drawn from the threads on the HVN and similar clinics this week.

1. CQC registration is not a quality rating. It means a service is registered and inspected. Look up the location on the CQC website and read the latest inspection report, not just the badge.
2. Ask for the GMC number of the doctor who will actually see you, and check it on the GMC register. A team page is not enough.
3. Ask who conducts the consultation and who would carry out any treatment.
4. Ask for the cancellation and refund terms in writing before you pay, including whether a consultation fee is credited if you go ahead.
5. For IV or NAD+ menus, ask which studies support each claimed benefit, what the known risks are, and what differs between price tiers.

I am not a doctor, and none of this replaces advice from your own clinician. Where I could not find good data, I have said so. What would you add to the list?", "post_id": 5}
{"comment_id": 4, "comment_like_id": 4}
